assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting artificial atom coupled to a microwave resonator into a controllable platform for strong light-matter coupling, dispersive readout and photon-mediated qubit interaction. It opened a genuinely new regime of microwave quantum optics and is the basis of most present superconducting quantum processors. It is original, clean, and has been reproduced by many laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf's 2004 proposal and the Wallraff et al. 2004 strong-coupling experiment form the core; Schoelkopf's group also drove the later cavity-based control and readout. The three credited names are a coherent theory-plus-experiment configuration, though Steven Girvin and others are not in the credited set and the division of credit between proposal and experiment is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently for roughly two decades and fully mature as physics. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so recognition of the cQED layer follows naturally and is timely rather than premature. Some overlap with the 2025 citation must be weighed.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits could be read as redundant by some members.
The credited set omits Steven Girvin and other proposal co-authors, so the fairest three-person configuration is debatable.
I work in this field and know the groups, so my assessment may be biased toward it; I flag this as a possible conflict of interest rather than independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, predicted to host flat bands and then shown to display correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity, created a tunable platform for strongly correlated physics and launched moire quantum materials. The discovery is original, clear and broadly influential.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011 continuum model predicted the magic angle; the Cao et al. 2018 experiments from the Jarillo-Herrero group demonstrated the correlated and superconducting states. Eva Andrei's earlier STM work on twisted graphene is also relevant and cannot be included in a three-person prize without displacing one of these three. Credit among experiment co-leaders (for example early authors) is not fully resolved.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced the main phases. The microscopic origin of the superconducting pairing is still debated, but the discovery itself is solid and the field is mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity remains unsettled.
Whether Andrei's contribution should displace a name from a three-person prize.
Sample-dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility of some phases.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, followed by experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells and 3D materials, established a new classification of band insulators with protected edge and surface states. This is a conceptually deep and lasting discovery.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental observation in HgTe wells (building on Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's prediction, who are not credited). Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is a fourth strong claim. A three-person limit forces a hard choice, and Zhang's death and the missing BHZ credit complicate fairness.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by multiple groups and materials for over fifteen years. Though the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions, this later development is distinct and well established.
uncertainties: Omitted claimants: Hasan from the credited set, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not credited at all.
Overlap in spirit with the 2016 prize on topological matter.
Applications remain limited despite strong fundamental impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide controllable quantum simulators of Hubbard-type models, from the Mott insulator transition to single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes. They give direct access to many-body physics that is hard to compute classically, and have changed how we study strongly correlated quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and coworkers proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition and later microscopy; Esslinger realised fermionic Hubbard physics, and Cirac contributed to the theory. Five credited names exceed the three-laureate limit, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and replicated worldwide. Earlier prizes recognised BEC (2001) and laser cooling, but this is a distinct step and is now ripe.
uncertainties: Which of five strong contributors should be omitted, and whether Jaksch (not credited) is critical.
Quantum simulation is still short of decisive advantage over classical methods for many problems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade, proposed as a route to fast neutral-atom gates, together with programmable tweezer arrays, enabled controlled many-body quantum simulation and gates with hundreds of atoms. It is a rapidly maturing platform with solid fundamental insight into strongly interacting Rydberg ensembles.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators proposed the blockade gate (Jaksch et al. 2000, Lukin et al. 2001); Browaeys and Lukin led the demonstrations of blockade and programmable arrays; Saffman contributed gate demonstrations and theory. The credited four names exceed three and the demarcation between proposal, early blockade experiments and array technology is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by several groups, but the field is still moving rapidly and the technological claims on fault-tolerant computing remain forward-looking. Somewhat early compared with the long-established candidates above.
uncertainties: Premature relative to settled work; the best-credit group may change within a few years.
Overlap with Zoller's other candidacies; the committee must avoid concentrating recognition on one theorist without reason.
Error-corrected computing claims are not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution, built on the BB84 protocol and Ekert's entanglement-based scheme, applied quantum mechanics to secure communication and helped trigger the field of quantum information. The ideas are clear and original, with lasting influence on the conceptual and applied side.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard and E91 by Ekert are the foundational contributions; Jian-Wei Pan's satellite and long-distance experiments are significant experimental credit but rest on the others' ideas. Three theorists is a clean configuration, but experimental recognition is omitted.
assessment.maturity: Protocols and implementations are confirmed over decades, though practical security (device and side-channel vulnerabilities) and real-world deployment are still evolving. The 2022 prize on entanglement tests partly overlaps.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement and Bell tests.
Whether the discovery is a physics advance or an information-theoretic or engineering one.
Experimental credit (Pan) may need to displace a theorist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fractional statistics of quasiparticles in two dimensions, predicted theoretically and detected via fractional charge and interferometric braiding experiments, is a fundamental extension of particle statistics and is relevant to topological quantum computing. It is conceptually deep.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim's 1977 work on identical particles in low dimensions is the theoretical origin of anyons (with Wilczek, who is not credited in this entry); Heiblum's shot-noise measurements of fractional charge and Feve's and Manfra's interferometry give experimental credit. The proposed trio mixes theory and experiment but the missing theorist and four experimental claimants make attribution contested.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is well confirmed; anyonic braiding statistics have recent interferometric and collision evidence from several groups, but the interpretation of some interferometer data remains under debate. Reasonably mature but not fully settled.
uncertainties: Wilczek, and Laughlin-related earlier prize credit, complicate attribution.
Interpretation of Fabry-Perot interferometer signatures and independent confirmation of non-Abelian cases is pending.
Fractional charge was largely recognised through the 1998 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical oscillators into the quantum regime through ground-state cooling, quantum-limited readout and entanglement of motion with light, creating a new platform for quantum control and sensing. It sits close to my own area of microwave and optical quantum circuits and is well-defined physics.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Painter are central leaders in optomechanics, but ground-state cooling and quantum-state control were also demonstrated in circuit-based electromechanics (Cleland, Lehnert, Teufel, Regal) and in LIGO-related work, so the three-person assignment is not unique.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across optical, microwave and mechanical platforms. Applications are still developing, and the single decisive discovery for a prize is less sharply defined than in higher-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: Which specific discovery would be cited, since the field has several parallel milestones.
Omitted contributors from electromechanics and early cooling work.
Impact beyond the field is still emerging.
